Field-induced Multi-𝑸→\boldsymbol{\vec{Q}} States in a Pyrochlore Heisenberg Magnet

Cecilie Glittum Affiliation: T.C.M. Group, Cavendish Laboratory, JJ Thomson Avenue, Cambridge CB3 0HE, United Kingdom Affiliation: Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin für Materialien und Energie GmbH, Hahn-Meitner-Platz 1 14109 Berlin, Germany Affiliation: Dahlem Center for Complex Quantum Systems and Fachbereich Physik, Freie Universität Berlin, 14195 Berlin, Germany    Olav F. Syljuåsen Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Oslo, P. O. Box 1048 Blindern, N-0316 Oslo, Norway
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We construct exact ground states of the J1J_{1}-J3​bJ_{3b} classical Heisenberg model on the pyrochlore lattice in the presence of a magnetic field. They are noncoplanar multi-Q→\vec{Q} spin configurations with a large magnetic unit cell that generalize the previously found coplanar sublattice pairing states. Using linear spin-wave theory, we show that entropy favors these multi-Q→\vec{Q} states at low temperatures in high magnetic fields. This is confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations, and a phase diagram is constructed. We also calculate the zero-temperature dynamical structure factor. Besides the usual Goldstone modes associated with the ordering Q→\vec{Q}s, we find high intensity gapless modes at momenta where there are no Bragg peaks.

I Introduction

Frustrated magnets, and particularly the highly frustrated pyrochlores, have garnered significant attention due to their predicted ability to host exotic states of matter, such as classical spin liquids. The antiferromagnetic (AF) nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model on the pyrochlore lattice is such a spin liquid due to its huge ground state degeneracy [1, 2, 3, 4]. This degeneracy is however lifted by further-neighbor couplings, and inclusion of second- and third-nearest neighbor couplings destabilize the spin liquid, inducing different kinds of order [5, 6, 7, 8].

While the primary interest in frustrated magnetism often lies in the lack of magnetic order in presence of strong correlations, i.e. spin liquidity, noncoplanar ordered states with several ordering wave vectors have also gained much attention, particularly due to their applications in spintronics [9, 10, 11]. Such multi-Q→\vec{Q} states are typically known to be realized in the presence of the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction [12, 13, 14]. However, they can also be stabilized by frustration [15], particularly with additional anisotropic exchange interactions [16, 17], impurities [18] or coupling to itinerant electrons [19, 20, 21]. These mechanisms are also known to induce multi-Q→\vec{Q} states on pyrochlore lattices [5, 6, 22, 7, 23, 24].

The third nearest-neighbor couplings are predicted to be the most important further-neighbor couplings in several pyrochlore materials [25, 26, 27]. For the pure AF J1J_{1}-J3​bJ_{3b} Heisenberg model (see Fig. 1), coplanar sublattice pairing (SLP) states are known to minimize the J1J_{1} and J3​bJ_{3b} energy terms simultaneously [8]. In these states, sublattices pair up antiferromagnetically, forming coplanar single-Q→\vec{Q} spirals corresponding to 120​°120\degree order in the triangular planes formed by the J3​bJ_{3b} coupling.

Here, we study the impact of an applied magnetic field on the pyrochlore AF J1J_{1}-J3​bJ_{3b} Heisenberg model. We start in Sec. II by constructing an ansatz for the system’s ground state as a generalized magnetic-field analog of the SLP ansatz of Ref. 8. This ansatz allows for a simultaneous SLP between all pairs of sublattices, and can describe more general states than the simple single-Q→\vec{Q} spiral on each sublattice. Instead, each sublattice has up to three ordering wave vectors, one for each sublattice pair. The system thus has up to six ordering wave vectors in total. In Sec. III, we present normalized multi-Q→\vec{Q} states satisfying the ansatz, and show further in Sec. IV that 6​Q→6\vec{Q}-states are favored entropically at sufficiently high magnetic fields. We define order parameters measuring various aspects of SLP order in Sec. V, and confirm our findings numerically using Monte Carlo (MC) simulations in Sec. VI, where we also map out the phase diagram. We compute zero-temperature static structure factors in Sec. VII and dynamical structure factors, i.e., spin waves, in Sec. VIII for selected values of the magnetic field, and end with a discussion of our findings in Sec. IX.

II Hamiltonian

We consider the following classical Heisenberg Hamiltonian in a magnetic field h→\vec{h} on the pyrochlore lattice

H\displaystyle H =J1​∑⟨r→,r→′⟩S→r→⋅S→r→′+J3​b​∑⟨⟨⟨r→,r→′⟩⟩⟩bS→r→⋅S→r→′−∑r→h→⋅S→r→,\displaystyle=J_{1}\!\!\sum_{\langle\vec{r},\vec{r}^{\,\prime}\rangle}\!\!\vec{S}_{\vec{r}}\cdot\vec{S}_{\vec{r}^{\,\prime}}+J_{3b}\!\!\!\!\!\!\sum_{\langle\langle\langle\vec{r},\vec{r}^{\,\prime}\rangle\rangle\rangle_{b}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\vec{S}_{\vec{r}}\cdot\vec{S}_{\vec{r}^{\,\prime}}-\sum_{\vec{r}}\vec{h}\cdot\vec{S}_{\vec{r}}, (1)

where the AF exchange couplings J1=1J_{1}=1 and J3​b>0J_{3b}>0 are illustrated in Fig. 1.

We begin by rewriting the Hamiltonian as

H=J12​∑t(S→t,0+S→t,1+S→t,2+S→t,3−4​m→)2+J3​b4∑s=03∑△(S→i0,s+S→i1,s+S→i2,s−3m→)2,\begin{split}H&=\frac{J_{1}}{2}\sum_{t}\left(\vec{S}_{t,0}+\vec{S}_{t,1}+\vec{S}_{t,2}+\vec{S}_{t,3}-4\vec{m}\right)^{2}\\ &+\frac{J_{3b}}{4}\sum_{s=0}^{3}\sum_{\triangle}\left(\vec{S}_{i_{0},s}+\vec{S}_{i_{1},s}+\vec{S}_{i_{2},s}-3\vec{m}\right)^{2},\end{split} (2)

where the first sum goes over all up and down tetrahedra tt of the lattice, of which there are N/2N/2 (NN is the number of spins), and S→t,s\vec{S}_{t,s} denotes the spin on tetrahedron tt and sublattice ss. The second sum goes over all elementary triangles on the triangular lattices formed by the J3​bJ_{3b} bonds, which couple spins on the same sublattice ss (see Fig. 1). The number of such triangles on each sublattice is also N/2N/2. The sites on each triangle are denoted i0,i1i_{0},i_{1} and i2i_{2}. We have subtracted a constant term coming from the spins and the average magnetization squared (m→\vec{m} is the average magnetization per spin). Multiplying out the parentheses, the resulting Hamiltonian is that of the J1J_{1}-J3​bJ_{3b} model in a magnetic field, where the magnetic field is along the axis of the magnetization and has magnitude h=(8​J1+9​J3​b)​mh=\left(8J_{1}+9J_{3b}\right)m. This gives a saturation field hsat=8​J1+9​J3​bh_{\rm sat}=8J_{1}+9J_{3b}, and an average magnetization per spin

m=h8​J1+9​J3​b.m=\frac{h}{8J_{1}+9J_{3b}}. (3)

The ground state energy (the constant we subtracted earlier) per spin is

EGSN=−(J1+32​J3​b+h22​(8​J1+9​J3​b)).\frac{E_{\rm GS}}{N}=-\left(J_{1}+\frac{3}{2}J_{3b}+\frac{h^{2}}{2(8J_{1}+9J_{3b})}\right). (4)

In Eq. (2), we have chosen to write the Hamiltonian so that the lowest energy is achieved when the spins satisfy

S→t,0+S→t,1+S→t,2+S→t,3=4​m→\vec{S}_{t,0}+\vec{S}_{t,1}+\vec{S}_{t,2}+\vec{S}_{t,3}=4\vec{m} (5)

for each tetrahedron and

S→i0,s+S→i1,s+S→i2,s=3​m→\vec{S}_{i_{0},s}+\vec{S}_{i_{1},s}+\vec{S}_{i_{2},s}=3\vec{m} (6)

for each triangle. We will refer to Eq. (5) (Eq. (6)) as the tetrahedron (triangle) condition. The rationale behind this choice is to match it with known results in the cases J1>0,J3​b=0J_{1}>0,J_{3b}=0 [28] and J1=0J_{1}=0,J3​b>0J_{3b}>0 [29].

II.1 Ansatz

In the following, we label the spins by either their face-centered cubic (fcc) lattice point R→\vec{R} and sublattice index i={0,1,2,3}i=\{0,1,2,3\}, or their position r→=R→+δ→i\vec{r}=\vec{R}+\vec{\delta}_{i}. R→\vec{R} describes the position of an up tetrahedron and is constructed from the fcc primitive lattice vectors a→1=(0,1/2,1/2),a→2=(1/2,0,1/2)\vec{a}_{1}=(0,1/2,1/2),\vec{a}_{2}=(1/2,0,1/2), and a→3=(1/2,1/2,0)\vec{a}_{3}=(1/2,1/2,0), where we have set the cubic lattice constant to unity. The corresponding reciprocal lattice vectors are b→1=2​π​(−1,1,1)\vec{b}_{1}=2\pi(-1,1,1), b→2=2​π​(1,−1,1)\vec{b}_{2}=2\pi(1,-1,1), and b→3=2​π​(1,1,−1)\vec{b}_{3}=2\pi(1,1,-1). The sublattice vectors δ→i\vec{\delta}_{i}, which describe the spin positions on a single up tetrahedron, are δ→i=a→i/2\vec{\delta}_{i}=\vec{a}_{i}/2 for i={0,1,2,3}i=\{0,1,2,3\}, where we have defined a→0=(0,0,0)\vec{a}_{0}=(0,0,0).

A general ansatz satisfying the tetrahedron and triangle conditions is

S→R→,0=+u→01​cos⁡(Q→01⋅R→)+v→01​sin⁡(Q→01⋅R→)+u→02​cos⁡(Q→02⋅R→)+v→02​sin⁡(Q→02⋅R→)+u→03​cos⁡(Q→03⋅R→)+v→03​sin⁡(Q→03⋅R→)+m→,S→R→,1=−u→01​cos⁡(Q→01⋅R→)−v→01​sin⁡(Q→01⋅R→)+u→12​cos⁡(Q→12⋅R→)+v→12​sin⁡(Q→12⋅R→)+u→13​cos⁡(Q→13⋅R→)+v→13​sin⁡(Q→13⋅R→)+m→,S→R→,2=−u→02​cos⁡(Q→02⋅R→)−v→02​sin⁡(Q→02⋅R→)−u→12​cos⁡(Q→12⋅R→)−v→12​sin⁡(Q→12⋅R→)+u→23​cos⁡(Q→23⋅R→)+v→23​sin⁡(Q→23⋅R→)+m→,S→R→,3=−u→03​cos⁡(Q→03⋅R→)−v→03​sin⁡(Q→03⋅R→)−u→13​cos⁡(Q→13⋅R→)−v→13​sin⁡(Q→13⋅R→)−u→23​cos⁡(Q→23⋅R→)−v→23​sin⁡(Q→23⋅R→)+m→,\begin{split}\vec{S}_{\vec{R},0}=&+\vec{u}_{01}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{01}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{v}_{01}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{01}\cdot\vec{R})}\\ &+\vec{u}_{02}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{02}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{v}_{02}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{02}\cdot\vec{R})}\\ &+\vec{u}_{03}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{03}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{v}_{03}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{03}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{m},\\ \vec{S}_{\vec{R},1}=&-\vec{u}_{01}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{01}\cdot\vec{R})}-\vec{v}_{01}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{01}\cdot\vec{R})}\\ &+\vec{u}_{12}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{12}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{v}_{12}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{12}\cdot\vec{R})}\\ &+\vec{u}_{13}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{13}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{v}_{13}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{13}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{m},\\ \vec{S}_{\vec{R},2}=&-\vec{u}_{02}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{02}\cdot\vec{R})}-\vec{v}_{02}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{02}\cdot\vec{R})}\\ &-\vec{u}_{12}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{12}\cdot\vec{R})}-\vec{v}_{12}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{12}\cdot\vec{R})}\\ &+\vec{u}_{23}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{23}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{v}_{23}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{23}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{m},\\ \vec{S}_{\vec{R},3}=&-\vec{u}_{03}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{03}\cdot\vec{R})}-\vec{v}_{03}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{03}\cdot\vec{R})}\\ &-\vec{u}_{13}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{13}\cdot\vec{R})}-\vec{v}_{13}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{13}\cdot\vec{R})}\\ &-\vec{u}_{23}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{23}\cdot\vec{R})}-\vec{v}_{23}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{23}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{m},\end{split} (7)

where the wave vectors Q→i​j\vec{Q}_{ij} are listed in Table 1. Note that the minus signs in the ansatz cause an antiparallel tendency of spins on pairs of sublattices, hence we term this ansatz the SLP ansatz.

The choice of minus signs gives S→R→,0+S→R→,1+S→R→,2+S→R→,3=4​m→\vec{S}_{\vec{R},0}+\vec{S}_{\vec{R},1}+\vec{S}_{\vec{R},2}+\vec{S}_{\vec{R},3}=4\vec{m}, meaning that the tetrahedron condition is satisfied for all up tetrahedra. The tetrahedron condition is also satisfied for the down tetrahedra, ∑iS→R→−a→i,i=4​m→\sum_{i}\vec{S}_{\vec{R}-\vec{a}_{i},i}=4\vec{m}. This can be seen by letting R→→R→−a→i\vec{R}\to\vec{R}-\vec{a}_{i} on sublattice ii. It gives the same cancellations as for the up tetrahedra, which follows from Q→i​j⋅a→i=Q→i​j⋅a→j\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{a}_{i}=\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{a}_{j}, as one can easily check by inspecting Table 1.

To see that also the triangle condition is satisfied, it is necessary to divide each sublattice into parallel triangular J3​bJ_{3b} planes (as shown for one of the sublattices in Fig. 1), and furthermore, divide each triangular plane into trisublattices, such that an elementary triangle has one site from each trisublattice. A possible way of doing this is to introduce integer-valued plane and trisublattice indices, PP and TT, respectively, as defined in Table 2. When rewriting the SLP ansatz in Eq. (7) with this labeling, we find that the particular choices of Q→i​j\vec{Q}_{ij}s in Table 1 cause all trigonometric functions to have arguments which depend on the trisublattice index as 2​π​T/32\pi T/3 and on the plane index as 2​π​P/32\pi P/3. Therefore, for each elementary triangle in a given plane, the trigonometric functions from the different trisublattices cancel each other, and the triangle condition is satisfied. We also note that there are at most three different planes on a given sublattice, which follows from the 2​π​P/32\pi P/3 dependence, making the spin configuration periodic when PP changes by 3.

III Ground states

Since the SLP ansatz in Eq. (7) fulfills both the tetrahedron and triangle conditions, any proper state satisfying the ansatz is a ground state of the Hamiltonian. To be a proper classical spin state, each spin must have unit length. It is in general difficult to achieve this for multi-Q→\vec{Q} states, as they often have a large number of different spins in the unit cell and a corresponding large number of normalization constraints. Here, the Q→i​j\vec{Q}_{ij}s make any spin configuration that obeys Eq. (7) periodic with unit cell (3​a→1,3​a→2,3​a→3)(3\vec{a}_{1},3\vec{a}_{2},3\vec{a}_{3}), with a total of 108 spins. However, only 36 of these spins can be different, nine on each sublattice (at most three different planes with three spins each on each sublattice), giving rise to 36 normalization constraints. These are listed in Appendix A.

The general SLP ansatz, Eq. (7), allows for several solutions that fulfill the length constraints. It is not the purpose here to find all solutions, but rather to describe a selected set that is most likely to be realized in finite-temperature systems.

III.1 Zero field

In zero field, the simplest solution to the normalization constraints is the coplanar solution introduced in Ref. 8. It amounts to setting all u→\vec{u}’s and v→\vec{v}’s to zero except u→01⟂v→01\vec{u}_{01}\perp\vec{v}_{01} and u→23⟂v→23\vec{u}_{23}\perp\vec{v}_{23}, which are all unit vectors. Explicitly, it is

S→R→,0=+u→01​cos⁡(Q→01⋅R→)+v→01​sin⁡(Q→01⋅R→),S→R→,1=−u→01​cos⁡(Q→01⋅R→)−v→01​sin⁡(Q→01⋅R→),S→R→,2=+u→23​cos⁡(Q→23⋅R→)+v→23​sin⁡(Q→23⋅R→),S→R→,3=−u→23​cos⁡(Q→23⋅R→)−v→23​sin⁡(Q→23⋅R→).\begin{split}\vec{S}_{\vec{R},0}&=+\vec{u}_{01}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{01}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{v}_{01}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{01}\cdot\vec{R})},\\ \vec{S}_{\vec{R},1}&=-\vec{u}_{01}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{01}\cdot\vec{R})}-\vec{v}_{01}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{01}\cdot\vec{R})},\\ \vec{S}_{\vec{R},2}&=+\vec{u}_{23}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{23}\cdot\vec{R})}+\vec{v}_{23}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{23}\cdot\vec{R})},\\ \vec{S}_{\vec{R},3}&=-\vec{u}_{23}\cos{(\vec{Q}_{23}\cdot\vec{R})}-\vec{v}_{23}\sin{(\vec{Q}_{23}\cdot\vec{R})}.\end{split} (8)

This corresponds to sublattice pairing (01)&(23)(01)\&(23). Other sublattice pairings ((02)&(13)(02)\&(13) and (03)&(12)(03)\&(12)) are also possible. In this state, the three coplanar spins on a particular plane and sublattice are constructed from a single wave vector Q→i​j\vec{Q}_{ij} (and its negative) and form a 120°arrangement which is the same for all planes on the given sublattice. We call this state SLP1, where the subscript refers to the number of different momenta Q→i​j\vec{Q}_{ij} on each sublattice (±Q→i​j\pm\vec{Q}_{ij} are considered equal in this respect). As a whole, SLP1 is a 2​Q→2\vec{Q}-state, as both Q→01\vec{Q}_{01} and Q→23\vec{Q}_{23} are present. This SLP1 state has the characteristic feature of antiparallel spins going along the a→0−a→1\vec{a}_{0}-\vec{a}_{1} and a→2−a→3\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{3} directions on sublattices 0,10,1 and 2,32,3, respectively. In Ref. 8, it was found that among the possible relative orientations of the spiral ordering vectors u→01\vec{u}_{01} and u→23\vec{u}_{23} (v→01\vec{v}_{01} and v→23\vec{v}_{23}), spin-wave fluctuations selects entropically the coplanar state u→01=u→23\vec{u}_{01}=\vec{u}_{23} and v→01=v→23\vec{v}_{01}=\vec{v}_{23}.

The coplanar SLP1 solution in Eq. (8) is a special case of a more general solution where the nonzero u→\vec{u}’s and v→\vec{v}’s are

u→01=u→23,v→01=v→23,v→02=v→12=v→03=−v→13,\displaystyle\vec{u}_{01}=\vec{u}_{23},\quad\vec{v}_{01}=\vec{v}_{23},\quad\vec{v}_{02}=\vec{v}_{12}=\vec{v}_{03}=-\vec{v}_{13}, (9)

with u→23\vec{u}_{23} being a unit vector that is perpendicular to two other unit vectors w→1\vec{w}_{1} and w→2\vec{w}_{2} which parametrize

v→13=(w→1+w→2)/3,v→23=(2​w→1−w→2)/3.\displaystyle\vec{v}_{13}=(\vec{w}_{1}+\vec{w}_{2})/3,\quad\vec{v}_{23}=(2\vec{w}_{1}-\vec{w}_{2})/3. (10)

The presence of the other v→\vec{v}’s in addition to v→01\vec{v}_{01} and v→23\vec{v}_{23} causes the appearance of all six momentum vectors Q→i​j\vec{Q}_{ij} in the spin configuration. Thus, this state is a 6​Q→6\vec{Q}-state when v→13≠0\vec{v}_{13}\neq 0. A general property of these states is that spins on sublattices 0 and 1 (2 and 3) with identical trisublattice and plane indices are antiparallel, and spins on sublattices 0 and 2 (1 and 3) with identical trisublattice and plane index are parallel. Additionally, the spins in one of the three planes on the same sublattice are in general different from the spins in the remaining two planes. Thus, the strict up-down alternation along directions a→0−a→1\vec{a}_{0}-\vec{a}_{1} and a→2−a→3\vec{a}_{2}-\vec{a}_{3} does in general no longer hold.

The special case w→1=−w→2\vec{w}_{1}=-\vec{w}_{2} implies v→13=0\vec{v}_{13}=0 and corresponds to the coplanar SLP1 solution above, where the three planes on each sublattice are equal. For w→1=w→2\vec{w}_{1}=\vec{w}_{2}, we find a coplanar state that differs slightly from SLP1. In this state, two spins on one of the triangular planes on every sublattice are permuted, so that the chirality of the 120°arrangement in that plane is opposite to the remaining two planes.

For noncollinear arrangements of w→1\vec{w}_{1} and w→2\vec{w}_{2}, one gets a noncoplanar spin state. Because of the noncoplanarity, we expect this state to have smaller entropy than the coplanar SLP1 state, and less likely to be realized at finite temperatures.

III.2 Finite field

In a finite magnetic field, the general zero-field solution Eqs. (9,10) gives unit length spins if u→23,w→1\vec{u}_{23},\vec{w}_{1} and w→2\vec{w}_{2} are modified to be vectors of length 1−m2\sqrt{1-m^{2}} perpendicular (⟂\perp) to the field. This implies a configuration where the ⟂\perp-components of the spins with identical trisublattice and plane indices are antiparallel on sublattices 0 and 1 (2 and 3) and parallel on sublattices 0 and 2 (1 and 3). The components parallel (     ) to the field of all the spins are identical and equal to the magnetization per spin mm. However, since the vectors u→23\vec{u}_{23}, w→1\vec{w}_{1} and w→2\vec{w}_{2} lie in the plane perpendicular to the magnetic field and u→23\vec{u}_{23} must be perpendicular to both w→1\vec{w}_{1} and w→2\vec{w}_{2}, there are only two possibilities for w→1\vec{w}_{1} and w→2\vec{w}_{2} given u→23\vec{u}_{23}. In the first case, the w→\vec{w}’s are antiparallel, giving a canted version of SLP1. This state is essentially SLP1 within the ⟂\perp-plane, but with all spins having the same finite      -component (see Fig. 1). The other case, parallel w→\vec{w}’s, gives similarly a canted version of the zero-field state where one plane of spins has an opposite chirality in-plane 120°arrangement than in the other two planes.

The previously discussed noncoplanar zero-field solutions have no analog in a magnetic field. However, there are other classes of solutions which resemble the previous ones in that any spin on a given sublattice is “antiparallel” to one spin on two of the other sublattices (in a field we use the term “antiparallel” for two spins having opposite ⟂\perp-components and equal      -components) and parallel to a spin on the remaining sublattice. Such solutions are more likely to have high entropy due to the high number of (anti)parallel spins. We have found one particularly interesting example of this, where spins that are ‘‘antiparallel’’ do no longer have equal plane indices, as was the case for the solutions discussed previously. Instead, the spins in planes (0,1,2)(0,1,2) on sublattice 0 (2) are “antiparallel” to the spins of equal trisublattice index in planes (0,2,1)(0,2,1) on sublattice 1 (3), which leads to

u12⟂=−u03⟂,\displaystyle u_{12}^{\perp}=-u_{03}^{\perp},\;\; u12=+u03,\displaystyle u_{12}^{{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}}=+u_{03}^{{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}},
v12⟂=+v03⟂,\displaystyle v_{12}^{\perp}=+v_{03}^{\perp},\;\; v12=−v03,\displaystyle v_{12}^{{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}}=-v_{03}^{{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}},
u13⟂=−u02⟂,\displaystyle u_{13}^{\perp}=-u_{02}^{\perp},\;\; u13=+u02,\displaystyle u_{13}^{{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}}=+u_{02}^{{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}},
v13⟂=−v02⟂,\displaystyle v_{13}^{\perp}=-v_{02}^{\perp},\;\; v13=+v02,\displaystyle v_{13}^{{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}}=+v_{02}^{{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}},
u01=0,v01=0,\displaystyle u_{01}^{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}=0,\;\;v_{01}^{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}=0,\;\; u23=0,v23=0.\displaystyle u_{23}^{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}=0,\;\;v_{23}^{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}=0.

Further, the spins on sublattices 0 (1) and 2 (3) are parallel for equal plane and trisublattice indices, implying

u→02\displaystyle\vec{u}_{02} =0,\displaystyle=0,
u03\displaystyle u_{03}^{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu} =0,v03=0,\displaystyle=0,\;\;\;\;\;v_{03}^{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}=0,
u→23\displaystyle\vec{u}_{23} =u→01,v→23=v→01.\displaystyle=\vec{u}_{01},\;\;\vec{v}_{23}=\vec{v}_{01}.

This leaves us with only two vectors with finite      -components: v→02\vec{v}_{02} and v→13\vec{v}_{13}. The remaining u→\vec{u}’s and v→\vec{v}’s all lie in the ⟂\perp-plane.

Even with these conditions, there are many solutions. However, solutions different from those already classified have v→02⟂=0\vec{v}_{02}^{\perp}=0. The normalization problem then reduces to nine equations (normalization of the nine spins on sublattice zero) with eleven unknowns. We solve these nine equations, leaving the direction of u→01\vec{u}_{01} and the angle α−π/2\alpha-\pi/2 between u→01\vec{u}_{01} and u→03\vec{u}_{03} as free parameters. We find that u→01\vec{u}_{01} (u→03\vec{u}_{03}) and v→01\vec{v}_{01} (v→03\vec{v}_{03}) must be orthogonal vectors of length a+b\sqrt{a+b} (a−b\sqrt{a-b}), where

a\displaystyle a =12​(1−m2−8​m2​tan2⁡α),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(1-m^{2}-8m^{2}\tan^{2}\alpha),
b\displaystyle b =12​(1−m2)2−16​m2​(1+3​m2)​tan2⁡α.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{(1-m^{2})^{2}-16m^{2}(1+3m^{2})\tan^{2}\alpha}.

Additionally, the directions of v→01\vec{v}_{01} and v→03\vec{v}_{03} must be chosen to satisfy

u→01⋅v→03\displaystyle\vec{u}_{01}\cdot\vec{v}_{03} =u→03⋅v→01.\displaystyle=\vec{u}_{03}\cdot\vec{v}_{01}.

The nonzero component of v→02\vec{v}_{02} is v02 ​ =−4​|m→|​tan⁡αv_{02}^{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}=-4|\vec{m}|\tan\alpha. Lastly, the angle α\alpha is restricted by

α∈[0,αmax]∪[π−αmax,π],\alpha\in[0,\alpha_{\rm max}]\cup[\pi-\alpha_{\rm max},\pi], (11)

where

tan⁡αmax=1−m24​|m|​(1+3​m2).\tan\alpha_{\rm max}=\frac{1-m^{2}}{4|m|\sqrt{(1+3m^{2})}}. (12)

For α={0,π}\alpha=\{0,\pi\}, this solution is the canted SLP1 state with u→012=1−m2\vec{u}_{01}^{2}=1-m^{2} and u→032=v→022=0\vec{u}_{03}^{2}=\vec{v}_{02}^{2}=0. As α\alpha is increased (decreased) from 00 (π\pi), the canted SLP1 state continuously evolves into a state where each sublattice has three Q→\vec{Q}s; SLP3,α (with six Q→\vec{Q}s in total). In this state, there is a different order in each of the three triangular planes on a given sublattice. An explicit parametrization of this SLP3,α state is shown in Appendix B. The value αmax\alpha_{\rm max} gives the “maximal” SLP3,α state, where |u→01|=|u→03||\vec{u}_{01}|=|\vec{u}_{03}|. We will refer to this as the SLP3,M state (see Fig. 2).

In the SLP3,α states, the spin components along the magnetic field take three values: {m,m⁡(1±2​3​tan⁡α)}\{m,m(1\pm 2\sqrt{3}\tan{\alpha})\}. This is a consequence of only v→02\vec{v}_{02} and v→13\vec{v}_{13} having a finite      -component. For α={0,π}\alpha=\{0,\pi\}, all spin      -components become equal to mm (canted SLP1). The difference in the three values along the field increases as α\alpha approaches αmax\alpha_{\rm max}.

Taking the limit m→0m\to 0, we note that SLP3,α approaches the coplanar single-Q→\vec{Q} SLP1 state for all α≠αmax\alpha\neq\alpha_{\rm max}, while for α=αmax\alpha=\alpha_{\rm max}, we instead get a noncoplanar zero-field analog of the SLP3,M state, different from the previously discussed zero-field solutions.

We note that other solutions similar to SLP3,α can be found by transforming R→\vec{R} according to the lattice symmetries. This will lead to solutions with other pairings of “antiparallel” and parallel planes and trisublattice indices, depending on the transformation.

IV Spin-wave entropy

For a given value of the magnetic field, all states described by the ansatz in Eq. (7) have equal energies. To determine which of these are favored at finite temperatures, we compute their entropy using linear spin-wave theory. We assign each particular ground state to a periodic fcc system with the unit cell of M=33×4=108M=3^{3}\times 4=108 spins. The spin configurations define site-dependent rotated frames, in terms of which the spins are in a ferromagnetic configuration. We then use the Holstein-Primakoff [30] transformation to describe the deviations from the ferromagnetic configuration as bosons. The resulting boson Hamiltonian is expanded to quadratic order, with vanishing linear terms. This Hamiltonian is then diagonalized numerically to obtain the spin-wave frequencies ωq→,i\omega_{\vec{q},i}, using a Bogoliubov transformation involving 2​M2M bosons [31]. We regularize the zero modes by adding a small value 10−1010^{-10} to the diagonal of the Hamiltonian matrix. For further details, see Appendix C.

The entropy per site from these linear spin-wave fluctuations can then be computed as

S/N=−1l3​M∑q→∑i=1Mlnωq→,i,S/N=-\frac{1}{l^{3}M}\sum_{\vec{q}}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\ln{\omega_{\vec{q},i}}, (13)

where the sum over q→\vec{q} goes over the first Brillouin zone of the lattice with l3l^{3} MM-site unit cells. In order to find the entropy for l→∞l\to\infty, we compute the entropy for sizes l={6,9,12,15,18}l=\{6,9,12,15,18\} and extrapolate S/NS/N versus 1/l31/l^{3} to infinite size using a quadratic polynomial. We use the parameter values J1=1J_{1}=1, J3​b=0.2J_{3b}=0.2.

In zero magnetic field, the ground states are parametrized by three unit vectors: u→23,w→1\vec{u}_{23},\vec{w}_{1} and w→2\vec{w}_{2}, where u→23\vec{u}_{23} is perpendicular to w→1\vec{w}_{1} and w→2\vec{w}_{2}. We label the angle between w→1\vec{w}_{1} and w→2\vec{w}_{2} as θ\theta. Then, computing the entropy for these solutions, we get the results shown in Fig. 3. The maximal entropy occurs for θ=π\theta=\pi, which corresponds to the coplanar SLP1 solution.

For the zero-field SLP3,M state, we find eight gapless modes, compared to 14 for the coplanar SLP1 state. Thus, we conclude that the coplanar SLP1 solution also has higher entropy than the zero-field SLP3,M state.

For finite fields, the entropy per site for SLP3,α as a function of α\alpha, is shown in Fig. 4. The Bogoliubov diagonalizations for these configurations yield four gapless modes. It is seen that for low fields (h<4h<4), the entropy is maximal for α=0\alpha=0, corresponding to the canted SLP1 state. For higher fields (h>4h>4), the entropy is instead maximal for α=αmax\alpha=\alpha_{\rm max}, corresponding to SLP3,M. Figure 4 also shows that the change between these two values (00 and αmax\alpha_{\rm max}) at h=4h=4 is discontinuous.

To better see that the change happens at h=4h=4, we compare the values of the entropy per site versus magnetic field for the two α\alpha values in Fig. 5.

V Order parameters

To distinguish the SLP1 state from the SLP3 states in the subsequent numerics, we construct four order parameters. For the first order parameter, we make use of the fact that the SLP1 state can be viewed as two sets of crossing parallel chains where the spins on each chain are ordered in an “antiparallel” way. In an SLP1 state with (01)&(23)(01)\&(23) pairing, one set of chains runs along the direction a→1−a→0\vec{a}_{1}-\vec{a}_{0} involving alternate sublattice 0 and 1 sites. The other set runs along the direction a→3−a→2\vec{a}_{3}-\vec{a}_{2} and involves sites on the sublattices 2 and 3 (see Fig. 1). For one chain involving sublattices ii and jj, we define the chain staggered order parameter as

C→R→0,i​j≡12​L​∑n(S→R→0+n⁡(a→j−a→i),i−S→R→0+n⁡(a→j−a→i),j),\vec{C}_{\vec{R}_{0},ij}\equiv\frac{1}{2L}\sum_{n}\left(\vec{S}_{\vec{R}_{0}+n(\vec{a}_{j}-\vec{a}_{i}),i}-\vec{S}_{\vec{R}_{0}+n(\vec{a}_{j}-\vec{a}_{i}),j}\right), (14)

where R→0\vec{R}_{0} is an arbitrary up tetrahedron on the chain. LL is the linear size of the system such that the total number of spins is N=4​L3N=4L^{3}. We take the average length of this over all chains, which is achieved by taking the average over all up tetrahedra in the lattice

Ci​j2≡1L3​∑R→0C→R→0,i​j⋅C→R→0,i​j.C^{2}_{ij}\equiv\frac{1}{L^{3}}\sum_{\vec{R}_{0}}\vec{C}_{\vec{R}_{0},ij}\cdot\vec{C}_{\vec{R}_{0},ij}. (15)

From this, we construct the three-component complex SLP order parameter, OSLPO_{\rm SLP}, where each component corresponds to a particular way of pairing the sublattices,

OSLP=C01​C23+ei​2​π/3​C02​C13+ei​4​π/3​C03​C12.O_{\rm SLP}=C_{01}C_{23}+e^{i2\pi/3}C_{02}C_{13}+e^{i4\pi/3}C_{03}C_{12}. (16)

In the MC simulations, we measure all the Ci​jC_{ij}s and compute the modulus |OSLP||O_{\rm SLP}|. A nonzero value will be taken as an indicator of an SLP phase. In Appendix D it is shown that for a state respecting the SLP ansatz in Eq. (7),

Ci​j2=12​(u→i​j2+v→i​j2)C^{2}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\vec{u}_{ij}^{2}+\vec{v}_{ij}^{2}\right) (17)

and

|OSLP|\displaystyle|O_{\rm SLP}| =(1−m→2)2−3​(C012​C022+C012​C032+C022​C032).\displaystyle=\sqrt{\left(1-\vec{m}^{2}\right)^{2}-3\left(C^{2}_{01}C^{2}_{02}+C^{2}_{01}C^{2}_{03}+C^{2}_{02}C^{2}_{03}\right)}. (18)

The maximum value occurs for the canted SLP1 state, where only one of C01C_{01}, C02C_{02} and C03C_{03} is nonzero, giving

|OSLP,1|\displaystyle|O_{{\rm SLP},1}| =1−m2.\displaystyle=1-m^{2}. (19)

In the SLP3,M state, we get

|OSLP,M|\displaystyle|O_{{\rm SLP},M}| =|(1−m2)​(1−9​m2)4​(1+3​m2)|.\displaystyle=\left|\frac{(1-m^{2})(1-9m^{2})}{4(1+3m^{2})}\right|. (20)

Another property of the canted SLP1 state is that all spin      -components are equal. To detect deviations from this, we calculate the spatial fluctuations of the magnetization in the field-direction

κ≡1N​∑r→(Sr→ ​ −m)2.\kappa\equiv\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\vec{r}}\left(S^{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu}_{\vec{r}}-m\right)^{2}. (21)

For the canted SLP1 state; κ=0\kappa=0, while for the SLP3,M state

κM=(1−m2)22​(1+3​m2).\kappa_{M}=\frac{(1-m^{2})^{2}}{2(1+3m^{2})}. (22)

SLP1 and SLP3,α can also be distinguished by only SLP3,α having a nonvanishing tetrahedral scalar chirality [32, 23]

Oχ=4N​∑R→χ⁡(R→),O_{\chi}=\frac{4}{N}\sum_{\vec{R}}\chi(\vec{R}), (23)

where χ⁡(R→)\chi(\vec{R}) is the sum of the chiralities for the four faces of the up tetrahedron at R→\vec{R}. The chirality of a face is computed such that its three spins are ordered in a counter-clockwise direction w.r.t. the outward face normal:

χ⁡(R→)=S→R→,1⋅(S→R→,2×S→R→,3)+S→R→,3⋅(S→R→,0×S→R→,1)+S→R→,0⋅(S→R→,3×S→R→,2)+S→R→,2⋅(S→R→,1×S→R→,0).\displaystyle\begin{split}\chi(\vec{R})&=\vec{S}_{\vec{R},1}\cdot(\vec{S}_{\vec{R},2}\times\vec{S}_{\vec{R},3})+\vec{S}_{\vec{R},3}\cdot(\vec{S}_{\vec{R},0}\times\vec{S}_{\vec{R},1})\\ \quad&+\vec{S}_{\vec{R},0}\cdot(\vec{S}_{\vec{R},3}\times\vec{S}_{\vec{R},2})+\vec{S}_{\vec{R},2}\cdot(\vec{S}_{\vec{R},1}\times\vec{S}_{\vec{R},0}).\end{split} (24)

For the SLP3,α state, Oχ=2​(4​m​tan⁡α)3O_{\chi}=2\left(4m\tan{\alpha}\right)^{3}, which means that it is zero for the canted SLP1 state (α=0\alpha=0) and

Oχ,M=2​(1−m21+3​m2)3O_{\chi,M}=2\left(\frac{1-m^{2}}{\sqrt{1+3m^{2}}}\right)^{3} (25)

for SLP3,M.

A way to detect ordered multi-Q→\vec{Q} states is to measure the product of the static structure factors at the different ordering wave vectors. The static structure factor

Sμ​ν​(q→)≡12​(S−q→μ​Sq→ν+S−q→ν​Sq→μ)S^{\mu\nu}(\vec{q})\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left(S^{\mu}_{-\vec{q}}S^{\nu}_{\vec{q}}+S^{\nu}_{-\vec{q}}S^{\mu}_{\vec{q}}\right) (26)

is defined in terms of the Fourier transform Sq→μS^{\mu}_{\vec{q}} of the spin state. We define the (isotropic) 3​Q→3\vec{Q} (on each sublattice) order parameter which detects simultaneous ordering at Q→01\vec{Q}_{01}, Q→02\vec{Q}_{02} and Q→03\vec{Q}_{03} in the 111 Brillouin zone as

O3​Q→=1N3​(Sλ​λ​(Q→01+G→′)​Sμ​μ​(Q→02+G→′)​Sν​ν​(Q→03+G→′))1/2,O_{3\vec{Q}}=\frac{1}{N^{3}}\left(S^{\lambda\lambda}(\vec{Q}_{01}+\vec{G}^{\prime})S^{\mu\mu}(\vec{Q}_{02}+\vec{G}^{\prime})S^{\nu\nu}(\vec{Q}_{03}+\vec{G}^{\prime})\right)^{1/2}, (27)

where repeated Greek indices are summed over, and G→′≡b→1+b→2+b→3\vec{G}^{\prime}\equiv\vec{b}_{1}+\vec{b}_{2}+\vec{b}_{3}. O3​Q→O_{3\vec{Q}} is zero in the SLP1 phase, and nonzero in SLP3 phases; see Sec. VII.

VI Numerical Results

To get an independent confirmation of our analytical results, we have performed classical MC simulations on systems with an fcc lattice of tetrahedra with periodic boundary conditions. The simulations were carried out using multiple MC update types. In all our simulations one MC step consisted of NN single-spin Metropolis moves [33], where for each spin the proposed new random direction is restricted to lie in a cone about the old spin [34, 35, 36], NN over-relaxation moves [34] where a random spin is rotated an arbitrary angle about the effective magnetic field seen on its site, a number of Wolff-cluster updates [37] where clusters are formed of spins that will be mirrored on an arbitrary plane that includes the magnetic field direction (so that S ​ S^{\mkern 3.0mu\vphantom{\perp}\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 2.0mu\vrule depth=0.0pt\mkern 3.0mu} does not change), and 3​N3N single-spin Metropolis moves where the cartesian spin components, Sx,SyS^{x},S^{y} and SzS^{z}, of a single spin is attempted reversed. In some of the simulations, in addition to the above MC updates, we also implemented the parallel tempering setup [38] with a feedback-optimized scheme [39] to select a set of temperatures that cause as many round-trips as possible for each replica. The parallel tempering simulations were run with a fixed number of typically 20-50 replicas spanning a fixed temperature interval, with more replicas if the system is large in order to increase the replica swapping rate.

In the following we will show results for the parameter values J1=1J_{1}=1 and J3​b=0.2J_{3b}=0.2. The MC results shown in the figures (except Fig. 8) are mean values of 10-20 statistically independent bins, and the error bars mark the standard deviation of the mean. Where not visible, the error bars are smaller than the symbol size.

All our low-temperature numerical simulations show results consistent with the magnetization relation Eq. (3) and ground state energy Eq. (4), confirming the form of the Hamiltonian in Eq. (2).

In Fig. 6, we show parallel tempering MC results for |OSLP||O_{\rm SLP}| versus temperature TT in zero magnetic field for three different linear system sizes LL (N=4​L3N=4L^{3}). The SLP order parameter shows a steep increase at Tc=0.180T_{c}=0.180, which is 8%8\% lower than estimated using nematic bond theory [8]. The system size dependence of the critical temperature is weak, and the rise of the order parameter resembles that of a discontinuous phase transition, in accordance with the nematic bond theory results. When extrapolating to zero temperature, the SLP order parameter appears to reach the value 1, consistent with the low-temperature phase being the SLP1 state (with thermal fluctuations).

When a magnetic field is added, the MC simulations are in general more difficult to equilibrate. Using a system size of L=6L=6, we show in Fig. 7 the SLP order parameter versus temperature for different values of the magnetic field. The sharp rise of the SLP order parameter that was seen for zero field is still present for fields h≲4.5h\lesssim 4.5, and it appears to extrapolate to a value close to 1−m21-m^{2} as T→0T\to 0, shown as colored horizontal bars on the ordinate axis. This is consistent with the low-temperature phase being the canted SLP1 state. The associated critical temperature decreases as the magnetic field is increased.

We also observe from Fig. 7 that for small fields, h≲2.5h\lesssim 2.5, the system goes directly from the high-temperature disordered phase into the canted SLP1 phase at low temperatures. In contrast, for 2.5≲h≲4.52.5\lesssim h\lesssim 4.5 coming from high temperatures, there is first a slight increase in the SLP order parameter before it slightly decreases, and then increases sharply at a lower temperature (see the h=4h=4 curve in Fig. 7). For h≳4.5h\gtrsim 4.5 we find only the slight increase in the SLP order parameter, and no dramatic upturn down to the lowest temperatures studied (T>0.02T>0.02). Instead, the SLP order parameter extrapolates to a value close to that for the SLP3,M state when TT goes to zero, shown as crosses on the ordinate axis. We thus interpret the slight increase of the SLP order parameter as entering the SLP3,M phase and the more pronounced increase as entering the SLP1 phase.

To investigate the stability of the canted SLP1 state in a magnetic field at low temperatures, we have carried out long standard MC simulations without parallel tempering, all started from the canted SLP1 state. They were run for 10910^{9} MC steps, each at a fixed temperature. In Fig. 8, we show the spatial magnetization fluctuations κ\kappa (scaled by the expected value κM\kappa_{M} in the SLP3,M state) for ten independent simulations at each temperature and field value. It is apparent that for h=5h=5, all simulations have escaped the initial SLP1 state. Most of them (circles) get a value for κ\kappa which comes very close to the SLP3,M value when T→0T\to 0. There are also runs with slightly smaller values of κ\kappa (crosses), that are further distinguished from the others (circles) by having at least an order of magnitude smaller chirality |Oχ||O_{\chi}|.

Taking the final h=5h=5 spin configurations of these runs, and exposing them to an energy relaxation procedure, we relax the spin configurations to the corresponding ground state (relaxed energies differ from Eq. (4) by at most 10−1210^{-12}). We find that the spin configurations corresponding to higher κ\kappa relax to SLP3,M, while the ones with smaller κ\kappa attain a similar, but more complicated noncoplanar 6​Q→6\vec{Q} zero chirality configuration,SLP3,χ=0, that satisfies the ansatz Eq. (7), and has “antiparallel” spin pairs, but which is still not among the solutions outlined in Sec. III. While the chirality on individual up tetrahedra are generally nonzero in this state, their sum is zero. We have calculated the entropy per site of such zero chirality states for a range of field values, and find that it is lower than that of SLP3,M up to very high fields, h≃9.0h\simeq 9.0. Thus, we expect that finite temperature entropy selection will eventually prefer the SLP3,M state for even longer MC runs as long as h≲9.0h\lesssim 9.0. For higher magnetic fields the linear spin-wave entropies of the zero chirality state and the SLP3,M state are almost equal. For h=3h=3, κ\kappa goes to zero as T→0T\to 0 for all runs. This is consistent with SLP1, which is also what the energy relaxation procedure on these states shows.

The phase transition into the SLP1 state at zero magnetic field is discontinuous. This is also the case for small magnetic fields as shown in Fig. 9, where we show the energy per site at h=2.5h=2.5 versus temperature for different system sizes obtained using the parallel tempering method. At T≃0.175T\simeq 0.175 the curves develop with system size into a “knee” discontinuity, indicating a first order phase transition. In contrast to the zero field case, significant finite size effects are seen at h=2.5h=2.5 and it is therefore necessary to carry out simulations on larger lattices to map out the phase diagram. To do so, we employ the mixed phase technique [40] where fixed temperature MC simulations are started in a configuration where half of a large L=24L=24 system is in the canted SLP1 state and the other half in the SLP3,M state. The runs are relatively short, ∼104\sim 10^{4} MC steps, and the error bars are gotten from repeating the simulations five times with different random seeds. Figure 10 shows the SLP order parameter, the chirality order parameter, and the 3​Q→3\vec{Q} order parameter as functions of magnetic field for a fixed low temperature (T=0.075)(T=0.075). For h<3.8h<3.8 the SLP order parameter is large, and both the chirality and the 3​Q→3\vec{Q} order parameters are zero, consistent with the SLP1 phase. For h=3.8h=3.8 the 3​Q→3\vec{Q} order parameter makes a jump and then decreases with increasing field and vanishes at h=7.85h=7.85. The SLP order parameter is also finite in this region but smaller than in the SLP1 phase. The chirality order parameter also jumps at h=3.8h=3.8 and decreases until h=6.55h=6.55 at which it disappears abruptly, see Fig. 10 inset. We interpret this as phase transitions from SLP1 to SLP3,M at h=3.8h=3.8, from SLP3,M into SLP3,χ=0 at h=6.55h=6.55 and from SLP3,χ=0 to a disordered phase at h=7.85h=7.85. We have repeated these mixed phase simulations for other temperatures and also for temperature scans at fixed fields to obtain the phase diagram shown in Fig. 11, where the phase boundaries are gotten from sharp jumps in the order parameters and/or energy. From the energy versus TT curves in the mixed phase simulations, and also Fig. 9, we infer that the phase transitions to the disordered state are discontinuous. No such energy discontinuities were observed between the ordered phases.

VII Static structure factors

The ordered SLP states cause Bragg peaks in the static structure factors, Eq. (26), which can be measured in neutron scattering experiments. Using the SLP ansatz, Eq. (7), we compute the longitudinal structure factor analytically (taking h→\vec{h} along the zz-axis), giving

Sz​z(q→)=N232∑G→{∑i<j(ui​jz​2+vi​jz​2)Θ[G→⋅(a→i−a→j)]\displaystyle S^{zz}(\vec{q})=\frac{N^{2}}{32}\sum_{\vec{G}}\left\{\vphantom{\frac{1}{2}}\right.\sum_{i<j}\left(u^{z2}_{ij}+v^{z2}_{ij}\right)\Theta\!\left[\vec{G}\cdot(\vec{a}_{i}-\vec{a}_{j})\right]
×(δq→,G→+Q→i​j+δq→,−G→−Q→i​j)\displaystyle\times\left(\delta_{\vec{q},\vec{G}+\vec{Q}_{ij}}+\delta_{\vec{q},-\vec{G}-\vec{Q}_{ij}}\right) (28)
+2mz​2|1+ei​G→⋅a→1/2+ei​G→⋅a→2/2+ei​G→⋅a→3/2|2δq→,G→},\displaystyle+2m^{z2}\left|1+e^{i\vec{G}\cdot\vec{a}_{1}/2}+e^{i\vec{G}\cdot\vec{a}_{2}/2}+e^{i\vec{G}\cdot\vec{a}_{3}/2}\right|^{2}\delta_{\vec{q},\vec{G}}\left.\vphantom{\frac{1}{2}}\right\},

where Θ⁡[G→⋅(a→i−a→j)]≡1−cos⁡(π⁡(ki−kj))\Theta[\vec{G}\cdot(\vec{a}_{i}-\vec{a}_{j})]\equiv 1-\cos{(\pi(k_{i}-k_{j}))}, G→=k1​b→1+k2​b→2+k3​b→3\vec{G}=k_{1}\vec{b}_{1}+k_{2}\vec{b}_{2}+k_{3}\vec{b}_{3} denotes reciprocal lattice vectors of the fcc Bravais lattice, and k0=0k_{0}=0 . The transverse structure factor, (Sx​x​(q→)+Sy​y​(q→))/2(S^{xx}(\vec{q})+S^{yy}(\vec{q}))/2 is similar, but with xx- and yy-components instead of zz and no mm-term.

It follows that only the longitudinal structure factor has peaks at Brillouin zone centers Γ\Gamma. In Brillouin zones where all kik_{i}s are even, the Γ\Gamma peak has magnitude (N​m)2\left(Nm\right)^{2} reflecting the total magnetization squared, and in Brillouin zones where k1+k2+k3k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3} is odd, the Γ\Gamma peak has magnitude (N​m/2)2\left(Nm/2\right)^{2}. In other Brillouin zones, there is no peak at Γ\Gamma.

The Θ\Theta-factor causes peaks at Q→i​j\vec{Q}_{ij} to occur only in Brillouin zones where ki−kjk_{i}-k_{j} is odd. We define sets of momenta

Q¯i​j≡{Q→i​j+k1​b→1+k2​b→2+k3​b→3},∀ki−kj∈odd.\bar{Q}_{ij}\equiv\{\vec{Q}_{ij}+k_{1}\vec{b}_{1}+k_{2}\vec{b}_{2}+k_{3}\vec{b}_{3}\},\;\;\forall\;k_{i}-k_{j}\in\mbox{odd}. (29)

where these peaks occur. Their peak intensities are

Sμ​ν​(q→∈±Q¯i​j)\displaystyle S^{\mu\nu}(\vec{q}\in\pm\bar{Q}_{ij}) =(N4)2​(ui​jμ​ui​jν+vi​jμ​vi​jν).\displaystyle=\left(\frac{N}{4}\right)^{2}\left(u^{\mu}_{ij}u^{\nu}_{ij}+v^{\mu}_{ij}v^{\nu}_{ij}\right). (30)

In Fig. 12, we show the static structure factors for the SLP1 and SLP3,M states as a function of field. We have not calculated it for SLP3,χ=0 as we do not have an analytic expression for that state.

VIII Dynamical structure factors

From the linear spin-wave calculation outlined in Sec. IV and Appendix C, we compute the zero-temperature dynamical structure factor

Sμ​ν(q→,ω)=∫−∞∞dt∑r→,r→′⟨Sr→μ(t)Sr→′ν(0)⟩e−iq→⋅(r→−r→′)ei​ω​t.S^{\mu\nu}(\vec{q},\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\!\!dt\sum_{\vec{r},\vec{r}^{\,\prime}}\langle S^{\mu}_{\vec{r}}(t)S^{\nu}_{\vec{r}^{\,\prime}}(0)\rangle e^{-i\vec{q}\cdot\left(\vec{r}-\vec{r}^{\,\prime}\right)}e^{i\omega t}. (31)

To make plots of this, we approximate the delta-functions coming from the spin-wave calculation by Gaussians centered on the excitation frequency with a standard deviation 0.01, and plot the resulting intensity in the Brillouin zone centered at b→1+b→2+b→3\vec{b}_{1}+\vec{b}_{2}+\vec{b}_{3} (111 zone) along straight lines in momentum space going from −Ki​j-{\rm K}_{ij} through the zone center Γ\Gamma to Ki​j{\rm K}_{ij} (Q→i​j=8​Ki​j/9\vec{Q}_{ij}=8{\rm K}_{ij}/9).

We will refer to Sz​z​(q→,ω)S^{zz}(\vec{q},\omega) and (Sx​x​(q→,ω)+Sy​y​(q→,ω))/2(S^{xx}(\vec{q},\omega)+S^{yy}(\vec{q},\omega))/2 as the longitudinal and transverse dynamical structure factors, respectively. The dynamical structure factors are in general rather complex because of the large 108-site unit cell, so we focus the discussion on the lowest energy modes.

In Fig. 13, we show the transverse and longitudinal dynamical structure factors for the SLP1 state in zero magnetic field, Eq. (8), where u→01=u→23\vec{u}_{01}=\vec{u}_{23} and v→01=v→23\vec{v}_{01}=\vec{v}_{23} are chosen to lie in the x​yxy-plane. There are in total 14 different gapless modes. Two of these are associated with the transverse channel at Q¯01\bar{Q}_{01} and Q¯23\bar{Q}_{23}. They connect to the Bragg peaks at the same locations caused by the explicit appearance of Q→01\vec{Q}_{01} and Q→23\vec{Q}_{23} in the ground state configuration. The remaining 12 gapless modes are visible only in the longitudinal structure factor. They appear at all Q¯i​j\bar{Q}_{ij}s, although there are no associated longitudinal Bragg peaks. Four of these have spectral weights at ±Q¯01\pm\bar{Q}_{01} and ±Q¯23\pm\bar{Q}_{23}, four at ±Q¯02\pm\bar{Q}_{02} and ±Q¯13\pm\bar{Q}_{13} and the remaining four at ±Q¯03\pm\bar{Q}_{03} and ±Q¯12\pm\bar{Q}_{12}. Slightly away from each Q¯\bar{Q}, however, there are at most two distinct high-intensity low-energy spin-wave branches, dependent on the directions in momentum space. We list the numbers for selected directions D^\hat{D} in Table 3.

The 14 gapless modes can be explained by linearizing the length constraint equations in small deviations δ​u→i​j\delta\vec{u}_{ij} and δ​v→i​j\delta\vec{v}_{ij} from the planar SLP1 state. There are in total 36 independent δ​u→i​j\delta\vec{u}_{ij}- and δ​v→i​j\delta\vec{v}_{ij}-components. In zero field, the linearized equations reduce to 22 constraints, leaving us with 36−22=1436-22=14 gapless modes. The constraints require all ⟂\perp-components to be zero except for δ​u01y=−δ​v01x\delta u^{y}_{01}=-\delta v^{x}_{01} and δ​u23y=−δ​v23x\delta u^{y}_{23}=-\delta v^{x}_{23}. The two different transverse modes are therefore caused by the relative phase between the oscillations of the unpaired sublattices (e.g. 0 and 2) being either zero or π\pi (”scissor” mode), where the latter has the lowest energy. The remaining 12 modes are associated with modulations in the zz-direction associated with each of the 12 ui​jzu^{z}_{ij}’s and vi​jzv^{z}_{ij}’s.

When including small magnetic fields, the SLP1 ground state cants. In Fig. 14, we show the dynamical structure factor for such a canted SLP1 state when h=1h=1. There are four gapless modes. Two of these are visible as two low-energy spin-wave branches near Q¯01\bar{Q}_{01} and Q¯23\bar{Q}_{23} in the transverse channel, as discussed for zero field. The remaining two modes have strong intensities both at Q¯02\bar{Q}_{02} and Q¯13\bar{Q}_{13} in the longitudinal channel, and also at Q¯03\bar{Q}_{03} and Q¯12\bar{Q}_{12} in the transverse channel. Although there are two gapless modes at these momenta, we find that only one distinct band of low-energy excitations emanate out of them; depending on the direction, either only one mode is visible, or the two are degenerate. The four gapless modes can be explained by the four independent ways of deforming the canted SLP1 state to linear order without energy cost, as described by the linearized length constraint equations around the canted SLP1 solution:

δ​u01y\displaystyle\delta u_{01}^{y} =−δ​v01x,\displaystyle=-\delta v_{01}^{x}, (32)
δ​u23y\displaystyle\delta u_{23}^{y} =−δ​v23x,\displaystyle=-\delta v_{23}^{x}, (33)
δ​u03x\displaystyle\delta u_{03}^{x} =−δ​v03y=δ​u12x=δ​v12y=m~​δ​u13z=−m~​δ​u02z,\displaystyle=-\delta v_{03}^{y}=\delta u_{12}^{x}=\delta v_{12}^{y}=\tilde{m}\delta u_{13}^{z}=-\tilde{m}\delta u_{02}^{z}, (34)
δ​u03y\displaystyle\delta u_{03}^{y} =δ​v03x=−δ​u12y=δ​v12x=m~​δ​v13z=m~​δ​v02z,\displaystyle=\delta v_{03}^{x}=-\delta u_{12}^{y}=\delta v_{12}^{x}=\tilde{m}\delta v_{13}^{z}=\tilde{m}\delta v_{02}^{z}, (35)

where m~≡m/1−m2\tilde{m}\equiv m/\sqrt{1-m^{2}}, and all other components δ​u→i​j,δ​v→i​j\delta\vec{u}_{ij},\delta\vec{v}_{ij} are zero. In particular, the two last equations imply relations between the zz-components of δ​u→02\delta\vec{u}_{02} and δ​v→02\delta\vec{v}_{02} and the x​yxy-components of δ​u→03\delta\vec{u}_{03} and δ​v→03\delta\vec{v}_{03}, explaining why the gapless modes at Q¯02\bar{Q}_{02} and Q¯13\bar{Q}_{13} in the longitudinal channel also show up in the transverse channel at Q¯03\bar{Q}_{03} and Q¯12\bar{Q}_{12}.

For high magnetic field (h=5h=5) we calculate the dynamical structure factor for the SLP3,M state; see Fig. 15. It has more low-intensity spin-wave branches than SLP1. We find four gapless modes that are all dominantly transverse and each one has spectral weights on eight of the 12 different ±Q¯i​j\pm\bar{Q}_{ij}; two of the modes lack spectral weights on {±Q¯02,±Q¯13}\{\pm\bar{Q}_{02},\pm\bar{Q}_{13}\}, the third on {Q¯03,−Q¯01,−Q¯12,−Q¯23}\{\bar{Q}_{03},-\bar{Q}_{01},-\bar{Q}_{12},-\bar{Q}_{23}\}, and the fourth on {−Q¯03,Q¯01,Q¯12,Q¯23}\{-\bar{Q}_{03},\bar{Q}_{01},\bar{Q}_{12},\bar{Q}_{23}\}. Therefore there are at most two low-energy transverse spin-wave branches emanating out of ±Q¯02\pm\bar{Q}_{02} and ±Q¯13\pm\bar{Q}_{13}, and at most three for the other Q¯i​j\bar{Q}_{ij}s. Linearizing the constraint equations around the SLP3,M state, we find that all δ​ui​jz=δ​vi​jz=0\delta u^{z}_{ij}=\delta v^{z}_{ij}=0, which explains why the gapless modes lack spectral weight in the longitudinal channel. Furthermore the linearized equations give δ​u02⟂=δ​u13⟂=0\delta u_{02}^{\perp}=\delta u_{13}^{\perp}=0, and conditions where the in-plane components δ​ui​j⟂\delta u^{\perp}_{ij} and δ​vi​j⟂\delta v^{\perp}_{ij} with i​j={01,03,12,13,23}ij=\{01,03,12,13,23\} are parametrized by the four independent components of δ​v02⟂\delta v_{02}^{\perp} and δ​v03⟂\delta v_{03}^{\perp}. In particular, δ​v13⟂\delta v_{13}^{\perp} only depends on the two components of δ​v02⟂\delta v_{02}^{\perp}. From this, it follows that there are only two gapless modes at ±Q¯02\pm\bar{Q}_{02} and ±Q¯13\pm\bar{Q}_{13}.

The dynamical structure factors in Figs. 13-15 are only shown along −K0​i​Γ​K0​i-{\rm K}_{0i}\Gamma{\rm K}_{0i} in the 111 zone. The structure factor is identical in the 100 zone for i=1i=1, the 0​1¯​00\bar{1}0 zone for i=2i=2 and the 001 zone for i=3i=3. Additionally, it is identical for i=1i=1 along −K23​Γ​K23-{\rm K}_{23}\Gamma{\rm K}_{23} in the 001 and 010 zones with gapless modes at ±Q→23\pm\vec{Q}_{23} instead of ±Q→01\pm\vec{Q}_{01}, for i=2i=2 along −K13​Γ​K13-{\rm K}_{13}\Gamma{\rm K}_{13} in the 00​1¯00\bar{1} and 100 zones with gapless modes at ±Q→13\pm\vec{Q}_{13} and for i=3i=3 along −K12​Γ​K12-{\rm K}_{12}\Gamma{\rm K}_{12} in the 0​1¯​00\bar{1}0 and 1¯​00\bar{1}00 zones with gapless modes at ±Q→12\pm\vec{Q}_{12}. The remaining zones where ki−kjk_{i}-k_{j} are odd (101 and 110 for i​j=01,23ij=01,23, 011 and 110 for i​j=02,13ij=02,13, and 011 and 101 for i​j=03,12ij=03,12) have a generally different dynamical structure factor at high ω\omega, while the low-energy modes stay the same.

IX Discussion

In Ref. 8, SLP1 states were found to be the ground states of the classical pyrochlore Heisenberg antiferromagnet in zero magnetic field for an extended range of further-neighbor exchange interactions (with modified ordering wave vectors Q→i​j\vec{Q}_{ij}s). In these states, spins on pairs of sublattices form antiparallel coplanar spirals, and the ordering wave vectors for the two pairs are in general different. Here, we have found exact ground states for the pure AF J1J_{1}-J3​bJ_{3b} model in a magnetic field that generalize these SLP1 states.

Our key finding is that the ground states can be described by the SLP ansatz in Eq. (7). This ansatz ensures a spin sum of 4​m→4\vec{m} on every tetrahedron of J1J_{1} bonds, and 3​m→3\vec{m} on every elementary triangle of J3​bJ_{3b} bonds. It therefore describes ground states for all AF couplings J1,J3​b>0J_{1},J_{3b}>0. In the limits where either J3​b=0J_{3b}=0 or J1=0J_{1}=0, the SLP ansatz is however too restrictive as then only the tetrahedron condition or the triangle condition, respectively, should hold. For J3​b=0J_{3b}=0, i.e. the pure J1J_{1} model on the pyrochlore lattice in a magnetic field, the ground states constitute instead an extensive manifold with one degree of freedom per tetrahedron, i.e. N/2N/2 degrees of freedom in total [28]. In the opposite limit of J1=0J_{1}=0, the system reduces to decoupled triangular planes in a magnetic field for which the triangle condition should hold [41, 29]. This leaves three degrees of freedom for each triangular plane. Computations of the spin-wave entropy shows that the AF X​YXY model on the triangular lattice in a magnetic field favors the coplanar Y and 𝕍\mathbb{V} states [42], and MC simulations have shown that the corresponding Heisenberg model orders in the same phases at finite temperature [29, 43, 44]. The case studied here, where both J1J_{1} and J3​bJ_{3b} are nonzero, picks out the states which the two ground state manifolds have in common.

Our SLP ansatz generally describes spatially periodic multi-Q→\vec{Q} states with a large unit cell where the spins on pairs of sublattices have a tendency to be antiparallel in the plane perpendicular to the magnetic field and parallel along the field. However, the ansatz itself is incomplete as one also needs to choose its parameters such that all spins have unit length. Multi-Q→\vec{Q} states are typically incompatible with the unit length constraint. Nevertheless, we have here presented several normalized solutions. The simplest of these are the SLP1 states, that are identical to those found in Ref. 8 in zero magnetic field. In a finite magnetic field the coplanar SLP1 state smoothly goes into a canted SLP1 state that develops a uniform spin component along the magnetic field and stays almost unchanged in the plane perpendicular to the field. This SLP1 state is a 2​Q→2\vec{Q}-state. The SLP ansatz harbors also 6​Q→6\vec{Q}-states, but no normalizable 4​Q→4\vec{Q}-states (see Appendix E). Most interestingly, we have parametrized a family of states that interpolates continuously from the canted SLP1 state into 6​Q→6\vec{Q} SLP3 states, while keeping the spins normalized.

Finite temperatures induce an order-by-disorder mechanism favoring the state with the largest entropy. Using linear spin waves, we have calculated the entropy of the continuous family of SLP states. We find that for J1=1,J3​b=0.2J_{1}=1,J_{3b}=0.2, the canted SLP1 state is favored for magnetic fields h<4.0h<4.0, while the 6Q→\vec{Q}-state SLP3,M has the highest entropy for h>4.0h>4.0. The MC simulations indicate a slightly larger value for the zero-temperature critical field of this phase transition: hC≃4.15h_{C}\simeq 4.15 (see Fig. 11). The slight discrepancy with linear spin-wave theory is likely to be a finite size effect, but could also indicate a quantitative inadequacy of the linear spin-wave approximation. For the very highest magnetic fields we find that a 6​Q→6\vec{Q} state similar to SLP3,M but with zero up tetrahedron chirality, SLP3,χ=0, is realized in the MC simulations.

From the MC simulations, we conclude that the finite temperature disordering of the SLP1 and SLP3 phases are discontinuous. In addition, they indicate a magnetic field region (approximately h∈[2.5,9.1]h\in[2.5,9.1]) where the system exhibits multiple transitions as the temperature is lowered in a fixed magnetic field see Fig. 11. Lowering the field at a fixed temperature results also in multiple transitions except at the highest temperatures.

We have not been able to determine the specific thermodynamic nature of the boundaries between the ordered phases in Fig. 11, as we find no thermodynamic signatures associated with them. Thus they are likely rapid crossovers rather than true phase transitions. Nevertheless, as is evidenced by Fig. 10, the phases can be distinguished using a combination of order parameters and structure factors.

The ordered SLP states should exhibit Bragg peaks in neutron scattering experiments. We have calculated the static structure factors and find Bragg peaks at momenta corresponding to the ordering wave vectors in specific Brillouin zones, see Fig. 12. The discrimination between the SLP1 and SLP3 phases can then be made based on whether neutron scattering shows two or six inequivalent Bragg peaks at low temperatures in a single-domain single-crystalline material. Furthermore, the Bragg peaks for SLP1 should only be visible in the transverse channel, while SLP3 also shows peaks in the longitudinal channel.

We have also computed the spin-wave spectra of the SLP states and their corresponding dynamical structure factors. As is to be expected from a spin configuration with a large unit cell, the dynamical structure factor is rather complicated, having many spin-wave branches with different intensities. Focusing on the lowest energies, the dynamical structure factors reveal gapless modes at all momenta where there is a corresponding Bragg peak in the static structure factor. This is the usual scenario where the low energy spin waves describe long wavelength deformations of a spin configuration around its ordering wave vector. However, we also find additional high intensity gapless modes at momenta where there are no Bragg peaks.

In zero magnetic field, we find that the SLP1 state has in total 14 different gapless modes. This is many more than guaranteed by the Goldstone theorem, where the completely broken continuous O(3) symmetry at h=0h=0 leads to three gapless modes. Our results are however not in conflict with the Goldstone theorem, as it only gives a lower limit on the number of gapless modes. In fact, the number of gapless modes seen in the linear spin-wave calculation is in agreement with the number of independent solutions of the linearized spin normalization equations applied to the SLP ansatz. This indicates that the SLP ansatz is capable of describing all ground states in the vicinity of the SLP1 state. One can speculate about the fate of the 14 gapless modes when doing a higher order spin-wave calculation. As only three are protected by symmetry, many of them will probably become gapped.

For h≠0h\neq 0, we find four gapless modes for both the canted SLP1 and the SLP3,M states. This is again in agreement with the number of independent solutions to the linearized normalization equations of the SLP ansatz in a field. While we expect that a higher order spin-wave calculation will gap some of the modes, it is interesting to note that a particular nonlinear deformation of the spins should be expected to change the state according to what the interpolation parameter α\alpha would do (see Appendix B), thus maintaining zero energy even for nonlinear changes. The striking difference between the dynamical structure factors of the SLP1 and SLP3,M states is that the latter shows more intermediate intensity spin-wave branches. Yet, for neutron scattering experiments it might be more important that SLP1 has high-intensity low-energy longitudinal spin waves, while SLP3,M only has transverse.

Higher order spin-wave calculations should be able to describe magnon decays caused by cubic bosonic terms, which generally occur for noncollinear ground states [45, 46]. For a future study, it would be interesting to investigate how this affects the SLP1 and SLP3,M spin-wave spectra.

The J1J_{1}-J3​bJ_{3b} model studied here is believed to be relevant for the Gd2​B2​O7\mathrm{Gd}_{2}B_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7} class of materials (BB is a nonmagnetic cation) [25], however with additional dipole-dipole interactions [47, 48, 49]. While we have not considered dipole-dipole interactions, it would be interesting to study the effects of these and other interactions on our results. We note that other Heisenberg interactions were investigated in the zero-field case in Ref. 8. There, the SLP1 state survives when adding J2J_{2} and J3​aJ_{3a} as long as J1>J3​bJ_{1}>J_{3b} are both larger than J3​a−J2J_{3a}-J_{2}. Particularly, it would be interesting to study the stability of the collinear SLP-X phase found close to J3​b=J3​a−J2J_{3b}=J_{3a}-J_{2}, and possible multi-Q→\vec{Q} SLP3 analogs of this phase. This would be relevant for pyrochlore spinel materials [26, 27] and the breathing pyrochlore materials LiGaCr4​O8\mathrm{LiGaCr}_{4}\mathrm{O}_{8} and LiInCr4​O8\mathrm{LiInCr}_{4}\mathrm{O}_{8} [50]. As most of our results rely on satisfying the tetrahedron and triangle conditions, we expect that the accurate values of J1J_{1} and J3​bJ_{3b} are not important as long as they are both AF. Therefore, our results should apply also to breathing pyrochlores.

We hope that this work can lead to experimental searches for multi-Q→\vec{Q} ordered phases in pyrochlore magnets, and also inspire theoretical investigations of other 3D models of frustrated magnetism.

Appendix C Spin-wave expansion

The spin-wave expansion is carried out by first defining a rotated frame

Sr→α=Rr→α​β​Sr→′β,S^{\alpha}_{\vec{r}}=R_{\vec{r}}^{\alpha\beta}S^{\prime\beta}_{\vec{r}}, (36)

such that a ferromagnetic spin configuration along the zz-axis in the rotated frame is equal to the ground state spin configuration. In the rotated frame, we do a Holstein-Primakoff transformation [30] to expand around the ground state

(Sr→′xSr→′ySr→′z)=(S2​(ar→†+ar→)i​S2​(ar→†−ar→)S−ar→†​ar→).\begin{pmatrix}S^{\prime x}_{\vec{r}}\\ S^{\prime y}_{\vec{r}}\\ S^{\prime z}_{\vec{r}}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\frac{S}{2}}\left(a_{\vec{r}}^{\dagger}+a_{\vec{r}}\right)\\ i\sqrt{\frac{S}{2}}\left(a_{\vec{r}}^{\dagger}-a_{\vec{r}}\right)\\ S-a^{\dagger}_{\vec{r}}a_{\vec{r}}\end{pmatrix}. (37)

Inserting this into the Hamiltonian, the linear terms in boson operators vanish, and the quadratic part of the Hamiltonian becomes

H=12​∑q→Φq→†​Hq→​Φq→,H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\vec{q}}\Phi_{\vec{q}}^{\dagger}H_{\vec{q}}\Phi_{\vec{q}}, (38)

where q→\vec{q} runs over the first Brillouin zone of the lattice with an unit cell of M=4×33=108M=4\times 3^{3}=108 spins. Φq→=[aq→,1,⋯,aq→,M,a−q→,1†,⋯,a−q→,M†]T\Phi_{\vec{q}}=[a_{\vec{q},1},\cdots,a_{\vec{q},M},a^{\dagger}_{-\vec{q},1},\cdots,a^{\dagger}_{-\vec{q},M}]^{T} is a 2​M2M column vector of boson operators, and Hq→H_{\vec{q}} is a 2​M×2​M2M\times 2M matrix with coefficients coming from both the rotation matrices and the parameters of the original Hamiltonian.

Being boson operators, the components of Φq→\Phi_{\vec{q}} must obey the commutation relations

[Φq→,i,Φq→,j†]=gi​j,\left[\Phi_{\vec{q},i},\Phi^{\dagger}_{\vec{q},j}\right]=g_{ij}, (39)

where gg is a diagonal 2​M×2​M2M\times 2M matrix with +1+1 (−1)(-1) on the upper (lower) MM entries. To diagonalize the Hamiltonian, we define transformed bosons Ψ\Psi in the following way

Φq→=Tq→​Ψq→,\Phi_{\vec{q}}=T_{\vec{q}}\Psi_{\vec{q}}, (40)

where Tq→T_{\vec{q}} is a 2​M×2​M2M\times 2M matrix and Ψq→\Psi_{\vec{q}} is a 2​M2M column vector of transformed boson operators that also obey the commutation relations Eq. (39). This requirement leads to the following restriction on Tq→T_{\vec{q}}:

Tq→​g​Tq→†=g.T_{\vec{q}}\,gT^{\dagger}_{\vec{q}}=g. (41)

To diagonalize Hq→H_{\vec{q}} while maintaining this restriction, we follow Colpa [31] and decompose Hq→H_{\vec{q}} using a Cholesky decomposition Hq→=Kq→†​Kq→H_{\vec{q}}=K^{\dagger}_{\vec{q}}K_{\vec{q}}. Then the Hermitian matrix Kq→​g​Kq→†K_{\vec{q}}gK^{\dagger}_{\vec{q}} is diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are sorted in descending order and assigned to the diagonal matrix Dq→D_{\vec{q}}. We denote by Uq→U_{\vec{q}} the corresponding unitary matrix with eigenvectors of Kq→​g​Kq→†K_{\vec{q}}gK^{\dagger}_{\vec{q}} as columns. It then follows that

Tq→=Kq→−1​Uq→​g​Dq→,T_{\vec{q}}=K_{\vec{q}}^{-1}U_{\vec{q}}\sqrt{gD_{\vec{q}}}, (42)

which satisfies Eq. (41). The diagonal matrix of energy eigenvalues is

Eq→=Tq→†​Hq→​Tq→=g​Dq→.E_{\vec{q}}=T_{\vec{q}}^{\dagger}H_{\vec{q}}T_{\vec{q}}=gD_{\vec{q}}. (43)

Thus, the spin-wave frequencies at +q→+\vec{q} can be read off from the upper MM entries of g​DgD:

ωq→,i=Dq→i​i.\omega_{\vec{q},i}=D_{\vec{q}}^{ii}. (44)

This (para)diagonalization procedure fails if Hq→H_{\vec{q}} is not positive definite. Therefore, we add a small positive constant diagonal matrix to Hq→H_{\vec{q}} to keep the eigenvalues positive.

The dynamical structure factor is defined as

Sμ​ν(q→,ω)=∫−∞∞dt∑r→,r→′⟨Sr→μ(t)Sr→′ν(0)⟩e−iq→⋅(r→−r→′)ei​ω​t.S^{\mu\nu}(\vec{q},\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\!\!dt\sum_{\vec{r},\vec{r}^{\,\prime}}\langle S^{\mu}_{\vec{r}}(t)S^{\nu}_{\vec{r}^{\,\prime}}(0)\rangle e^{-i\vec{q}\cdot\left(\vec{r}-\vec{r}^{\,\prime}\right)}e^{i\omega t}. (45)

Inserting the rotation matrices and performing the Holstein-Primakoff transformation, keeping at most terms that are quadratic in the transformed boson operators, one can evaluate the boson correlators at zero temperature. Writing the transformation matrix Tq→T_{\vec{q}} on block-matrix form

Tq→=(Aq→Bq→Cq→Dq→)T_{\vec{q}}=\begin{pmatrix}A_{\vec{q}}&B_{\vec{q}}\\ C_{\vec{q}}&D_{\vec{q}}\end{pmatrix} (46)

and defining A~q→i​j≡e−iq→⋅δ→iAi​j\tilde{A}_{\vec{q}}^{ij}\equiv e^{-i\vec{q}\cdot\vec{\delta}_{i}}A^{ij} and C~q→i​j≡e−iq→⋅δ→iCi​j\tilde{C}_{\vec{q}}^{ij}\equiv e^{-i\vec{q}\cdot\vec{\delta}_{i}}C^{ij}, where δ→i\vec{\delta}_{i} is the position of the ii’th spin inside the unit cell, we arrive at the following expression for the dynamical structure factor

Sμ​ν​(q→,ω)=π​N​S​∑j=1Mδ⁡(ω−ωq→,j)×∑i,i′M[A~†j​i′q→(Ri′Λ1∗RTi)ν​μA~q→i​j+C~†j​i′q→(Ri′Λ1RTi)ν​μC~q→i​j+A~†j​i′q→(Ri′Λ2RTi)ν​μC~q→i​j+C~†j​i′q→(Ri′Λ2∗RTi)ν​μA~q→i​j],\begin{split}&S^{\mu\nu}(\vec{q},\omega)=\pi NS\sum_{j=1}^{M}\delta(\omega-\omega_{\vec{q},j})\\ &\times\sum_{i,i^{\prime}}^{M}\left[\tilde{A}^{\dagger ji^{\prime}}_{\vec{q}}\left(R_{i^{\prime}}\Lambda_{1}^{*}R^{T}_{i}\right)^{\nu\mu}\tilde{A}_{\vec{q}}^{ij}+\tilde{C}^{\dagger ji^{\prime}}_{\vec{q}}\left(R_{i^{\prime}}\Lambda_{1}R^{T}_{i}\right)^{\nu\mu}\tilde{C}_{\vec{q}}^{ij}\right.\\ &\left.+\tilde{A}^{\dagger ji^{\prime}}_{\vec{q}}\left(R_{i^{\prime}}\Lambda_{2}R^{T}_{i}\right)^{\nu\mu}\tilde{C}_{\vec{q}}^{ij}+\tilde{C}^{\dagger ji^{\prime}}_{\vec{q}}\left(R_{i^{\prime}}\Lambda_{2}^{*}R^{T}_{i}\right)^{\nu\mu}\tilde{A}_{\vec{q}}^{ij}\right],\end{split} (47)

where

Λ1=(1i0−i10000),Λ2=(1i0i−10000).\Lambda_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&i&0\\ -i&1&0\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\Lambda_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}1&i&0\\ i&-1&0\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.

Appendix D SLP order parameter

The SLP order parameter measures the staggered magnetization on chains along a→i−a→j\vec{a}_{i}-\vec{a}_{j}:

C→R→0,i​j≡12​L​∑n(S→R→0+n⁡(a→j−a→i),i−S→R→0+n⁡(a→j−a→i),j),\vec{C}_{\vec{R}_{0},ij}\equiv\frac{1}{2L}\sum_{n}\left(\vec{S}_{\vec{R}_{0}+n(\vec{a}_{j}-\vec{a}_{i}),i}-\vec{S}_{\vec{R}_{0}+n(\vec{a}_{j}-\vec{a}_{i}),j}\right), (48)

where R→0\vec{R}_{0} is an arbitrary up tetrahedron on the chain. Inserting the SLP ansatz, and performing the sum over nn, trigonometric terms with arguments 2​π​n/32\pi n/3 sum to zero (for LL divisible by 3). The only surviving terms are those with Q→i​j\vec{Q}_{ij} which follows from the fact that Q→i​j⋅(a→i−a→j)=0mod2​π{\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot(\vec{a}_{i}-\vec{a}_{j})=0\mod 2\pi}, ensuring that each term in the sum is independent of nn. This gives

C→R→0,i​j=u→i​j​cos⁡(Q→i​j⋅R→0)+v→i​j​sin⁡(Q→i​j⋅R→0).\vec{C}_{\vec{R}_{0},ij}=\vec{u}_{ij}\cos(\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{R}_{0})+\vec{v}_{ij}\sin(\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{R}_{0}). (49)

We then square this and take the average over all parallel chains. This is achieved by summing over all points on the fcc Bravais lattice

Ci​j2=1L3​∑R→0(u→i​j​cos⁡(Q→i​j⋅R→0)+v→i​j​sin⁡(Q→i​j⋅R→0))2.C^{2}_{ij}=\frac{1}{L^{3}}\sum_{\vec{R}_{0}}\left(\vec{u}_{ij}\cos(\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{R}_{0})+\vec{v}_{ij}\sin(\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{R}_{0})\right)^{2}. (50)

Performing this average, the trigonometric terms reduce to

1L3​∑R→0cos2⁡(Q→i​j⋅R→0)=12,\displaystyle\frac{1}{L^{3}}\sum_{\vec{R}_{0}}\cos^{2}(\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{R}_{0})=\frac{1}{2}, (51)
1L3​∑R→0sin2⁡(Q→i​j⋅R→0)=12,\displaystyle\frac{1}{L^{3}}\sum_{\vec{R}_{0}}\sin^{2}(\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{R}_{0})=\frac{1}{2}, (52)
1L3​∑R→0cos⁡(Q→i​j⋅R→0)​sin⁡(Q→i​j⋅R→0)=0,\displaystyle\frac{1}{L^{3}}\sum_{\vec{R}_{0}}\cos(\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{R}_{0})\sin(\vec{Q}_{ij}\cdot\vec{R}_{0})=0, (53)

implying that

Ci​j2=12​(u→i​j2+v→i​j2).C^{2}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\vec{u}_{ij}^{2}+\vec{v}_{ij}^{2}\right). (54)

Now by considering the length constraint equations for the spins on sublattice zero, one can show that they imply

u→012+v→012+u→022+v→022+u→032+v→032=2​(1−m→2).\vec{u}_{01}^{2}+\vec{v}_{01}^{2}+\vec{u}_{02}^{2}+\vec{v}_{02}^{2}+\vec{u}_{03}^{2}+\vec{v}_{03}^{2}=2(1-\vec{m}^{2}). (55)

Similar relations can be obtained for the other sublattices. Adding and subtracting these relations it follows that

u→012+v→012=u→232+v→232,\vec{u}_{01}^{2}+\vec{v}_{01}^{2}=\vec{u}_{23}^{2}+\vec{v}_{23}^{2}, (56)

which implies C23=C01C_{23}=C_{01}. Similarly, C13=C02C_{13}=C_{02} and C12=C03C_{12}=C_{03}. Therefore the three component complex order parameter, which captures also other sublattice pairings

OSLP=C01​C23+ei​2​π/3​C02​C13+ei​4​π/3​C03​C12O_{\rm SLP}=C_{01}C_{23}+e^{i2\pi/3}C_{02}C_{13}+e^{i4\pi/3}C_{03}C_{12}

becomes

OSLP\displaystyle O_{\rm SLP} =C012+ei​2​π/3​C022+ei​4​π/3​C032\displaystyle=C^{2}_{01}+e^{i2\pi/3}C^{2}_{02}+e^{i4\pi/3}C^{2}_{03}
=C012−12​(C022+C032)+32​i​(C022−C032).\displaystyle=C^{2}_{01}-\frac{1}{2}(C^{2}_{02}+C^{2}_{03})+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\left(C^{2}_{02}-C^{2}_{03}\right).

Squaring gives

|OSLP|2=(C012−12​(C022+C032))2+34​(C022−C032)2\displaystyle|O_{\rm SLP}|^{2}=\left(C^{2}_{01}-\frac{1}{2}(C^{2}_{02}+C^{2}_{03})\right)^{2}+\frac{3}{4}\left(C^{2}_{02}-C^{2}_{03}\right)^{2}
=(C012+C022+C032)2−3​(C012​C022+C012​C032+C022​C032).\displaystyle=\left(C^{2}_{01}+C^{2}_{02}+C^{2}_{03}\right)^{2}-3\left(C^{2}_{01}C^{2}_{02}+C^{2}_{01}C^{2}_{03}+C^{2}_{02}C^{2}_{03}\right).

Using Eq. (55), we get

|OSLP|\displaystyle|O_{\rm SLP}| =(1−m→2)2−3​(C012​C022+C012​C032+C022​C032).\displaystyle=\sqrt{\left(1-\vec{m}^{2}\right)^{2}-3\left(C^{2}_{01}C^{2}_{02}+C^{2}_{01}C^{2}_{03}+C^{2}_{02}C^{2}_{03}\right)}.

Appendix E Two wave vectors on a sublattice

We show in this section that the spins in an SLP state with two wave vectors on a sublattice, SLP2, cannot be normalized. Setting u→03=v→03=0\vec{u}_{03}=\vec{v}_{03}=0, the nine sublattice zero equations reduce to:

(u→01+u→02+m→)2\displaystyle\left(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}+\vec{m}\right)^{2} =1,\displaystyle=1, (57)
(u→01+u→02−2​m→)2+3​(v→01+v→02)2\displaystyle\left(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}-2\vec{m}\right)^{2}+3\left(\vec{v}_{01}+\vec{v}_{02}\right)^{2} =4,\displaystyle=4, (58)
(−2​u→01+u→02−2​m→)2+3​v→022\displaystyle\left(-2\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}-2\vec{m}\right)^{2}+3\vec{v}_{02}^{2} =4,\displaystyle=4, (59)
(u→01−2​u→02−2​m→)2+3​v→012\displaystyle\left(\vec{u}_{01}-2\vec{u}_{02}-2\vec{m}\right)^{2}+3\vec{v}_{01}^{2} =4,\displaystyle=4, (60)
(u→01+u→02−2​m→)2+3​(v→01−v→02)2\displaystyle\left(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}-2\vec{m}\right)^{2}+3\left(\vec{v}_{01}-\vec{v}_{02}\right)^{2} =4,\displaystyle=4, (61)
(u→01+u→02−2​m→)⋅v→01\displaystyle\left(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}-2\vec{m}\right)\cdot\vec{v}_{01} =0,\displaystyle=0, (62)
(u→01+u→02−2​m→)⋅v→02\displaystyle\left(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}-2\vec{m}\right)\cdot\vec{v}_{02} =0,\displaystyle=0, (63)
(u→01−2​u→02−2​m→)⋅v→01\displaystyle\left(\vec{u}_{01}-2\vec{u}_{02}-2\vec{m}\right)\cdot\vec{v}_{01} =0,\displaystyle=0, (64)
(−2​u→01+u→02−2​m→)⋅v→02\displaystyle\left(-2\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}-2\vec{m}\right)\cdot\vec{v}_{02} =0.\displaystyle=0. (65)

Equations (58) and (61) can be combined to give

v→01⋅v→02=0,\vec{v}_{01}\cdot\vec{v}_{02}=0, (66)

and the sum of Eqs. (59) and (60) combined with Eq. (57) gives

u→01⋅u→02=0.\vec{u}_{01}\cdot\vec{u}_{02}=0. (67)

If we now consider the planes spanned by these u→\vec{u}’s and v→\vec{v}’s, it follows from the orthogonality conditions that (u→01+u→02−2​m→)\left(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}-2\vec{m}\right) is a normal vector for the v→\vec{v}-plane. The remaining orthogonality conditions then give

u→01⋅v→02\displaystyle\vec{u}_{01}\cdot\vec{v}_{02} =0,\displaystyle=0, (68)
u→02⋅v→01\displaystyle\vec{u}_{02}\cdot\vec{v}_{01} =0.\displaystyle=0. (69)

The remaining length constraints give that

u→012+4​u→01⋅m→\displaystyle\vec{u}_{01}^{2}+4\vec{u}_{01}\cdot\vec{m} =v→012,\displaystyle=\vec{v}_{01}^{2}, (70)
u→022+4​u→02⋅m→\displaystyle\vec{u}_{02}^{2}+4\vec{u}_{02}\cdot\vec{m} =v→022,\displaystyle=\vec{v}_{02}^{2}, (71)

and

u→012+u→022+2​(u→01+u→02)⋅m→=1−m2.\vec{u}_{01}^{2}+\vec{u}_{02}^{2}+2(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02})\cdot\vec{m}=1-m^{2}. (72)

In zero magnetic field (m→=0\vec{m}=0), it is consequently impossible to normalize the spins. This is because (u→01+u→02)(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}) is the normal vector to the v→\vec{v}-plane (none of the vectors can have zero length, as that removes the corresponding Q→\vec{Q} because u→012=v→012\vec{u}_{01}^{2}=\vec{v}_{01}^{2} and u→022=v→022\vec{u}_{02}^{2}=\vec{v}_{02}^{2}). As v→02\vec{v}_{02} is perpendicular to u→01\vec{u}_{01} in addition to the v→\vec{v}-plane normal vector (u→01+u→02)(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}), v→02\vec{v}_{02} has to be normal to the u→\vec{u}-plane. However, as v→01\vec{v}_{01} is normal to v→02\vec{v}_{02} it follows that v→01\vec{v}_{01} lies in the u→\vec{u}-plane, but that breaks the condition that (u→01+u→02)(\vec{u}_{01}+\vec{u}_{02}) is normal to the v→\vec{v}-plane. The same conclusion holds also in the presence of a magnetic field as we have verified by direct insertion into the length constraint equations on all sublattices using Mathematica™.
